narrative: The model estimated your chance of bad credit at 45%. Although that is below 50%, it was above the lender’s approval threshold, so your application was denied. The decision was driven mainly by three factors. Your credit history was the strongest influence and pushed toward bad credit: your file shows no credits or all paid, a pattern held by only about 1% of approved applicants, whereas most approved applicants have existing paid credits. Your checking-account status was the second strongest influence and also pushed toward bad credit; a balance in the 0–200 DM range was less common among approved applicants—about 18% versus 59% with no balance listed. Working in your favour, the requested 12-month duration was shorter than the approved average of about 19 months, and this pushed toward good credit, but it was not enough to offset the first two concerns. To improve your position, ask the lender for the specific policy reason and whether a manual review is possible. Provide stable income and employment evidence, consider adding a guarantor or co-applicant, and build a clearer credit record—such as a small repaid loan or credit-building product—before reapplying. Improving your checking-account balance and savings would also strengthen a future application.
